subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 15! In this unit you will learn all about angles and movement – the maths of turning, facing, and finding your way. Every time you turn a corner on the way to the masjid, point towards the direction of the sunrise, or tell your friend how to reach the market, you are already using angles and directions. This unit will help you describe those turns and directions with clear, correct mathematics.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 3 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Explain that an angle is an amount of turn between two lines meeting at a point.
Identify and make a right angle (a quarter turn, or 90°), using tools such as a folded-paper corner or a set square to check it.
Compare angles to a right angle: greater than, less than, or equal to it.
Name the main types of angle: acute, right, obtuse and straight.
Use the four main compass points (North, East, South, West) and the four between them.
Describe turns as quarter, half, three-quarter and full turns.
Say whether a turn is clockwise or anticlockwise.
Follow and give directions for a route on a grid or simple map.
Read and describe a position on a labelled grid using column letters and row numbers (for example, the square C3).

concepts.title: What Is an Angle?
concepts.explanation: An angle is the amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point. Say that carefully to yourself: an angle is an amount of turn. It is not a shape, and it is not about how long the lines are. It is only about how far around you turn. Picture Hassan standing in the school yard. He points one arm straight ahead at the gate. Now he keeps his feet still and swings his arm around to point at the well. The amount his arm swept around is the angle. If he swings only a little, the angle is small. If he swings far around, the angle is large.
concepts.example: Every angle has these parts. The vertex is the point where the two lines meet. The arms are the two straight lines going out from the vertex. When you look at the corner of a page in your book, the very corner point is the vertex, and the two edges of the page going away from it are the arms.

concepts.title: The Right Angle
concepts.explanation:
The most important angle to know is the right angle. A right angle is a quarter turn – one quarter of the way around a full circle. Its size is 90°. A right angle makes a neat, square corner, shaped like the letter L.

Right angles are all around you. The corner of your book is a right angle. The corner of a window is a right angle. The corner of a door, a table, a tile on the floor, and a prayer mat – all right angles. A square and a rectangle each have four right angles, one at every corner. Once you start looking, you will see right angles everywhere in the buildings and objects around you.

You can make your very own right angle measure out of a piece of paper, and it works beautifully. Take any piece of paper, even one with rough, torn edges. Fold it in half once. Then fold it in half again so the first fold lines up neatly on top of itself. When you open it a little, the corner where the two folds meet is a perfect right angle. You made 90° with your own hands! You can hold this folded corner against any corner in the room to test whether it is a true right angle.
concepts.example: You can make your very own right angle measure out of a piece of paper, and it works beautifully. Take any piece of paper, even one with rough, torn edges. Fold it in half once. Then fold it in half again so the first… A folded-paper corner is a perfect homemade right-angle tester, but mathematicians and builders also use a real tool for this called a set square – a flat, triangular piece of plastic or metal with one perfectly square corner. To use a set square, place its square corner exactly into the corner you want to test: if the two straight edges of the set square line up neatly against the two sides of the corner with no gaps, the corner is a true right angle. A set square is also useful for drawing a right angle accurately on paper: place it on your page, draw along both of its short edges, and you will have drawn a perfect 90° corner every time.

concepts.title: Comparing Angles to a Right Angle
concepts.explanation:
Once you know the right angle well, you can use it to describe every other angle. We compare an angle to a right angle and ask a simple question: is it greater than, less than, or equal to a right angle? This gives us three families of angle.

A right angle is exactly equal to a right angle – it is exactly 90°, the square corner we already met.

An obtuse angle is greater than a right angle but still less than a straight line. It is bigger than 90° but smaller than 180°. Obtuse angles look wide and open, like a door opened far back or a book laid almost flat. Examples are 120° and 150°.

A straight angle is a special one: it is a half turn, exactly 180°, and its two arms make a single straight line. When Aisha stretches both arms straight out to her sides, one pointing left and one pointing right, her arms make a straight angle. A straight angle is the same as two right angles side by side.
concepts.example: You can test any angle against your paper right-angle measure. Place the corner of your folded paper into the angle. If the angle is smaller than your paper corner, it is acute. If it fits the paper corner exactly, it is a right angle. If the angle is wider and opens out past your paper corner, it is obtuse. This simple test lets you sort real angles into families without needing to measure the exact degrees. Try it on the corners around your home and see how many of each family you can find.

concepts.title: The Compass Points
concepts.explanation: A compass is a tool that helps us find our way. It shows us the main directions, called the compass points. The four main compass points are North, East, South and West. We use the short letters N, E, S and W. We can be more exact by adding four more directions between the main points. Between North and East is Northeast (NE). Between South and East is Southeast (SE). Between South and West is Southwest (SW). Between North and West is Northwest (NW). Now we have eight compass points, spaced equally around the circle.
concepts.example: The compass points connect directly to right angles and turns. Starting at North and turning clockwise, one right angle (a quarter turn) takes you to East. Another right angle takes you to South. Another takes you to West, and one more brings you back to North. So going all the way around passes through all four main points, using four right angles in total. This is why North, East, South and West are like the four square corners of a turning circle.

concepts.title: Turns – Quarter, Half, Three-Quarter and Full
concepts.explanation:
We describe how far something turns using four special turns. Each one is a number of right angles, so each one is easy to picture.

A quarter turn is one right angle. It is 90°. Example: turning from North to East.

A half turn is two right angles. It is 180°. Example: turning from North to South, so you end up facing the opposite way.

A three-quarter turn is three right angles. It is 270°. Example: turning from North all the way round to West.

A full turn is four right angles. It is 360°. Example: spinning around once until you face the very same way you started.

Notice the lovely pattern: each turn adds one more right angle. One right angle is a quarter turn, two is a half turn, three is a three-quarter turn, and four is a full turn that brings you home. This is why a full turn is 4 × 90° = 360°, and a half turn is 2 × 90° = 180°.

The best way to feel these turns is to stand up and try them with your own body. Face a wall and call it North. Make a quarter turn to your right – now you face a new wall, East. Make another quarter turn – you face the back of the room, South. Keep going and feel how a half turn always leaves you facing the exact opposite direction, and a full turn always brings you back to where you began. Sahra likes to practise this in the yard, calling out ‘quarter, half, three-quarter, full!’ as she spins.
concepts.example: Turns are useful for solving little puzzles. If Maryam faces North and makes a half turn, she faces South. If she then makes another quarter turn clockwise, she faces West. By breaking a big turn into right angles, you can always work out which way you end up facing. We will practise many of these puzzles later in the lesson.

concepts.title: Clockwise and Anticlockwise
concepts.explanation:
When something turns, it can turn in one of two directions. We use the words clockwise and anticlockwise to say which way.

Clockwise means turning the same way as the hands of a clock move. If you look at a clock on the wall, the hands go from the top, round to the right, then down, then to the left, and back to the top. Going through the compass points, clockwise is the order North, East, South, West and back to North.

Anticlockwise (sometimes called counterclockwise) means turning the opposite way to a clock's hands. Going through the compass points, anticlockwise is the order North, West, South, East and back to North. Anticlockwise is simply clockwise in reverse.

The direction of a turn matters a great deal. Suppose Abdi faces North and makes a quarter turn. If he turns clockwise, he ends up facing East. But if he turns anticlockwise, he ends up facing West instead – the opposite side! The size of the turn was the same quarter turn each time, but the direction changed where he finished. This is why we must always say both how much to turn and which way to turn.
concepts.example: Anticlockwise (sometimes called counterclockwise) means turning the opposite way to a clock's hands. Going through the compass points, anticlockwise is the order North, West, South, East and back to North. Anticlockwise… Direction words like clockwise and turns are perfect for describing a journey, but sometimes you need to describe exactly where something is without giving a journey at all – and for that, mathematicians use a labelled grid. A labelled grid is a grid of squares with columns labelled along the bottom, usually with letters (A, B, C, D…), and rows labelled up the side, usually with numbers (1, 2, 3, 4…). Every square on the grid has its own position, named by its column letter followed by its row number – for example, the square in column C and row 3 is called C3. To find a named square, run your finger across from the bottom until you reach the right letter, then up until you reach the right number, and the square where they meet is the one you want. Labelled grids like this are used on real maps to help you find a place quickly, in board games to say where a piece is standing, and in seating plans to find your exact seat.

methods.title: How to name an angle
methods.example: An angle is smaller than a right angle. What type of angle is it?
steps: Compare the angle to a right angle (use your paper measure).
If it is smaller than a right angle, it is acute.
If it fits exactly, it is a right angle (90°).
If it is wider but not a straight line, it is obtuse.
If its arms make a straight line, it is a straight angle (180°).

methods.title: How to work out a turn
methods.example: Is an angle of 120° greater than, less than, or equal to a right angle?
steps: Note which direction you start facing.
Note how big the turn is (quarter, half, three-quarter, full).
Note which way you turn (clockwise or anticlockwise).
Move one right angle at a time around the compass to find where you finish.

methods.title: How to follow a route on a grid
methods.example: Zahra is facing North. She makes a quarter turn clockwise. Which direction does she face now?
steps: Start at the given square, facing the given direction.
Do each instruction one at a time, in order.
After each move, say which way you now face and where you are.
Stop when you reach the finish and check it makes sense.

methods.title: A half turn
methods.example: Idris is facing East. He makes a half turn. Which direction does he face now?
steps: A half turn (180°) always leaves you facing the opposite direction.
The opposite of East is West.
So Idris faces West.
(It does not matter whether he turns clockwise or anticlockwise for a half turn — he ends up in the same place.)

methods.title: Direction matters
methods.example: Omar faces North and makes a quarter turn anticlockwise. Which direction does he face?
steps: Anticlockwise from North goes to West (the opposite way to clockwise).
So Omar faces West.
Compare this with Worked Example 3: the same size of turn, but the other direction, gives the opposite answer.

methods.title: Two turns in a row
methods.example: Maryam faces North. She makes a half turn, then a quarter turn clockwise. Which direction does she face at the end?
steps: Start North.
A half turn takes her to South.
A quarter turn clockwise from South takes her to West.
So Maryam finishes facing West.

workedExamples.title: Name the angle
workedExamples.prompt: An angle is smaller than a right angle. What type of angle is it?
workedExamples.solution: An angle smaller than a right angle (less than 90°) is an acute angle. Remember, acute angles are the small, sharp ones.

workedExamples.title: Compare to a right angle
workedExamples.prompt: Is an angle of 120° greater than, less than, or equal to a right angle?
workedExamples.solution: A right angle is 90°. Since 120° is more than 90°, the angle is greater than a right angle. Because it is more than 90° but less than 180°, it is an obtuse angle.

workedExamples.title: A quarter turn
workedExamples.prompt: Zahra is facing North. She makes a quarter turn clockwise. Which direction does she face now?
workedExamples.solution: Clockwise from North goes to East. So after a quarter turn clockwise, Zahra faces East.

workedExamples.title: A half turn
workedExamples.prompt: Idris is facing East. He makes a half turn. Which direction does he face now?
workedExamples.solution: A half turn (180°) always leaves you facing the opposite direction. The opposite of East is West. So Idris faces West. (It does not matter whether he turns clockwise or anticlockwise for a half turn — he ends up in the same place.)

workedExamples.title: Direction matters
workedExamples.prompt: Omar faces North and makes a quarter turn anticlockwise. Which direction does he face?
workedExamples.solution: Anticlockwise from North goes to West (the opposite way to clockwise). So Omar faces West. Compare this with Worked Example 3: the same size of turn, but the other direction, gives the opposite answer.

workedExamples.title: Two turns in a row
workedExamples.prompt: Maryam faces North. She makes a half turn, then a quarter turn clockwise. Which direction does she face at the end?
workedExamples.solution: Start North. A half turn takes her to South. A quarter turn clockwise from South takes her to West. So Maryam finishes facing West.

workedExamples.title: How many right angles?
workedExamples.prompt: A full turn is made of how many right angles, and how many degrees is that?
workedExamples.solution: A full turn is four right angles. Each right angle is 90°, so 4 × 90° = 360°. A full turn is 360°.

workedExamples.title: Follow a route
workedExamples.prompt: Hani starts at square (0, 0) facing North. She walks forward 3 squares, then makes a quarter turn clockwise and walks forward 4 squares. Which direction does she now face, and how far East has she moved?
workedExamples.solution: She walks 3 squares North first. Then a quarter turn clockwise from North makes her face East. She walks 4 squares East. So she now faces East and has moved 4 squares East (and 3 squares North from her start).

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: You face West and make a quarter turn anticlockwise. Which direction do you face?
workedExamples.solution: South (anticlockwise from West goes to South).

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: Fill the compass: between North and East is ___; between South and West is ___.

workedExamples.title: Which is the bigger turn each time
workedExamples.prompt: Which is the bigger turn each time: a) quarter turn or half turn b) three-quarter turn or full turn?
workedExamples.solution: a) half turn, b) full turn.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: You face East and make a three-quarter turn anticlockwise. Which direction do you face at the end?
workedExamples.solution: 1) East, three-quarter turn anticlockwise: East → North → West → South, so South.

activities.title: Fold Your Own Right-Angle Measure
steps: Take a piece of paper – even one with rough, torn edges works.
Fold it in half once, pressing the fold flat.
Fold it in half again so the first fold lies neatly on top of itself.
Open it slightly. The corner where the folds meet is a perfect right angle (90°).
Hold your right-angle corner against corners around the room to test which are true right angles.

activities.title: Right-Angle Hunt
activities.materials: your paper right-angle measure and a pencil.
steps: Walk around your home or classroom with your right-angle measure.
Find four true right angles (they fit your measure exactly). Draw them.
Find four angles that are greater than a right angle (obtuse). Draw them.
Find four angles that are less than a right angle (acute). Draw them.
Show a family member your collection and explain how you sorted each one.

activities.title: Compass Rose on the Floor
activities.materials: chalk, tape, or four labelled cards (N, E, S, W).
steps: Mark North, East, South and West on the floor, a right angle apart, like a big plus sign.
Stand in the middle facing North.
Call out a turn, such as ‘quarter turn clockwise’, and make it. Say which way you now face.
Try half turns and three-quarter turns. Check you land on the right direction each time.
Ask a partner to call the turns while you move, then swap over.

activities.title: Turn Game (Simon Says, Angles!)
activities.materials: yourself and one or more players.
steps: One player is the caller. They call turns like ‘Make a quarter turn anticlockwise!’
Everyone else makes the turn with their body.
The caller checks that everyone is facing the correct way.
Add compass points: ‘Face North!’ then ‘Now half turn – which way are you facing?’
Take turns being the caller. See who can follow the fastest without a mistake.

activities.title: Treasure Route Investigation
activities.materials: squared paper, a pencil, and a small object for ‘treasure’.
steps: Draw a grid of squares on your paper. Mark a START square and hide the ‘treasure’ on another square.
Write clear directions from START to the treasure using directions, turns and numbers of squares.
Give your directions to a partner and see if they reach the treasure.
Now find a different route to the same treasure and write those directions too.
How many different routes can you find? Record them and compare with a friend.

activities.title: Clock-Hand Angles (Family Task)
activities.materials: a clock with hands, or two strips of card pinned at one end to make ‘hands’.
steps: Set the hands to 3 o'clock. What type of angle do the hands make? (A right angle!)
Set them to 6 o'clock. What angle now? (A straight angle, 180°.)
Make an acute angle with the hands, then an obtuse angle.
Ask a family member to set an angle and challenge you to name it.
Talk about how the hands always turn clockwise – that is where the word comes from!

rules.title: Angle Rule
rules.text: An angle is the amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point. The length of the arms does not change the angle. Only the turn matters. We measure angles in degrees. A full turn is 360 degrees.

rules.title: Right-Angle Rule
rules.text: A right angle is a quarter turn. It is 90 degrees. It looks like a square corner (L). Two right angles make a straight line, 180 degrees (a half turn). Four right angles make a full turn, 360 degrees.

rules.title: Key rule 3
rules.text: Comparing Angles Acute angle: smaller than a right angle (less than 90 degrees). Right angle: exactly 90 degrees. Obtuse angle: bigger than a right angle but less than a straight line (90 to 180 degrees). Straight angle: a half turn, exactly 180 degrees.

rules.title: Key rule 4
rules.text: Turns and Directions Clockwise follows a clock: North to East to South to West. Anticlockwise is the opposite: North to West to South to East. Quarter turn = 90. Half turn = 180. Three-quarter turn = 270. Full turn = 360.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The first corner is a right angle; the wider corner is an obtuse angle.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Sahra says a full turn is the same as two half turns. Is she right? Explain using degrees.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Yes – a full turn is 360° and a half turn is 180°, and 180° + 180° = 360°, so two half turns make one full turn.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Clockwise and Anticlockwise.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: When something turns, it can turn in one of two directions. We use the words clockwise and anticlockwise to say which way. Clockwise means turning the same way as the hands of a clock move. If you look at a clock on the wall, the hands go from the top, round to the right, then down, then to the left, and back to the top. Going through the compass points, clockwise is the order North, East, South, West and back to North.

I can follow and give directions for a route on a grid or simple map.
